customers.title: Selling 1 — Customers & Selling Foundations
customers.desc: The customer master done right: groups, territories, contacts and addresses, credit limits, and the Selling Settings that shape every document after it.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Customer master, field by field
lessons.html:
Every quotation, sales order, delivery note and invoice in ZhiftERP begins with a question: who is this for? The answer is a Customer record, and the quality of that record decides the quality of everything that follows. A well-built customer master means documents that default correctly, statements that reconcile, credit that is controlled, and reports that answer management's questions without a single spreadsheet. A carelessly built one means the opposite, for years. This chapter walks the record field by field.

Creating the record. Navigate Selling > Customer > New (or press the plus from the Customer list). The form opens with the identity section on top. Before typing anything, understand the difference between the customer's name and the record's ID: what you type as Customer Name is the trading identity you'll see on documents; whether the system also uses it as the record's permanent ID, or issues a series number like CUST-00042 instead, is governed by Customer Naming By in Selling Settings (Chapter 7 and, in depth, Selling 8). For now: type the legal or trading name exactly, consistently cased — "Alpha Pharmacy Ltd", not "alpha pharm", not "ALPHA PHARMACY (Mr Chidi's one)".

Customer Type — Company or Individual. Companies carry registration and tax identity and typically several contacts; individuals are natural persons. The choice affects which identity fields make sense (a Tax ID belongs to a company) and how you'll structure contacts. Retail chains, distributors, corporates: Company. A walk-in professional buying on account: Individual. When in doubt for B2B trade, it's Company.

Customer Group. The first of the two great reporting dimensions. It answers what kind of customer this is — Retail, Pharmacy, Distributor, Corporate, Government — and every serious sales report can slice by it. Groups are covered as a design exercise in Chapter 2; at creation time the rule is simply: never leave the default unexamined. If your defaults chapter set "All Customer Groups" or a generic bucket, a lazily created customer disappears from segment analysis forever.

Territory. The second great dimension: where. Lagos Mainland, Lagos Island, Abuja FCT, South-West. Chapter 3 designs the tree; the creation-time rule mirrors groups: choose deliberately. And two anti-patterns to refuse on sight: a territory named after a salesperson (people resign; Ikeja does not), and a territory set to a warehouse (fulfilment geography is not sales geography).

Default Price List. Which set of selling rates this customer receives. When a quotation is raised for them, this list lands on the document and every row's rate is looked up from it (Selling 2 covers the machinery). Distributor customers point at the distributor list; retail at standard. Leave it blank and the global default from Selling Settings applies — acceptable for the common case, wrong for anyone on negotiated rates.

Default Currency. The currency their documents are priced and their receivable is tracked in. For domestic trade: NGN. For your Ghanaian or export relationships: the trading currency. The diagnostic habit to build now: when a customer's quotations keep defaulting to the wrong currency, the durable fix is this field on the master — editing each quotation treats the symptom and guarantees the disease recurs on the next document.

Tax identity. For Nigerian companies, record the Tax ID (TIN) — your FIRS e-invoicing pipeline (the NGE stack) and formal B2B invoicing both want it, and chasing TINs at invoice time is how billing stalls. Capture it at onboarding while the relationship is new and cooperative.

Accounts and terms (a preview). The master also carries the customer's default Payment Terms (Net 30, advance-and-balance — inherited by invoices, as Selling 7 teaches), their receivable account override if your chart demands one, and the Credit Limit section that Chapter 6 treats end-to-end. The principle across all of them: everything a document will need should already live on the master, so document creation is selection, not invention.

The creation discipline. A customer record is created once and transacted against for years. Create it deliberately: name, type, group, territory, currency, price list, TIN, terms — all set before the first quotation. "Only a name, details later" is the master-data equivalent of unhedged debt: later never comes, every document inherits blanks, and the dimensions you need at year-end were never captured. The master record is a contract with your future reports; sign it properly.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Customer Groups: designing the segmentation tree
lessons.html:
Customer Group is not a label; it is the backbone of every answer to "how is each part of our market doing?" This chapter treats it as what it is — a small piece of information architecture that deserves an hour of design before the first customer is created.

The mechanics. Customer Groups live in a tree (Selling > Customer Group, or the tree view). A group can be a group node (has children, holds no customers directly) or a leaf (customers attach here). Reports roll leaves up through their parents automatically: sales for "Pharmacy — Independent" and "Pharmacy — Chain" sum into "Pharmacy", which sums into "Healthcare", which sums into the root. You design the rollup once; every report inherits it forever.

Designing the tree — three rules.

  • Rule 1: one question per tree. The group tree answers what kind of customer. Resist the temptation to encode geography (that's Territory), size (consider a custom field or naming convention), or payment behaviour (that's credit data) into group names. "Lagos Pharmacies (Big, Slow-paying)" as a group is three dimensions crushed into one string — unreportable on any of them.
  • Rule 2: mirror how management actually talks. If the MD asks "how did Pharmacy do versus Distribution?", those are your top branches. A tree that mirrors the org's mental model gets used; a taxonomically "correct" tree nobody recognises gets ignored and defaulted around.
  • Rule 3: leaves you can assign in two seconds. Every real customer must land in exactly one obvious leaf. If your team debates where a customer goes, the tree is too clever. Six to fifteen leaves serves most Nigerian mid-market firms; thirty means you're encoding something that belongs elsewhere.

A worked tree for a ZhiftERP retail-systems vendor: All Customer Groups → Retail (→ Supermarket · Pharmacy · Specialty), Distribution (→ FMCG Distributor · Pharma Distributor), Corporate & Institutional, Government. Eight leaves, every prospect obviously placeable, every board question answerable by rollup.

Groups as machinery, not just reporting. The group is also a condition elsewhere in ZhiftERP: pricing rules can target a customer group ("10% off for Distribution", Selling 6), and defaults can hang from groups. That doubles the case for a clean tree — a pricing policy aimed at a mushy group hits mushy targets.

Changing your mind later. Re-parenting a group or moving a customer between leaves is allowed and takes effect in reports immediately (they read current assignments). What you cannot recover is history never captured: customers dumped for a year into a generic default have a year of unsegmentable sales. Hence the Chapter 1 discipline — the tree is only as good as assignment at creation time.

The default group. Selling Settings names a default group for hurried creation. Point it at your genuinely most common leaf — not at the root, and not at a "Misc" bucket that becomes a landfill. A weekly two-minute review of newly created customers (filter by creation date) catches misfiled ones while they're young.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Territories: geography as a reporting dimension
lessons.html:
Territory answers where. Like groups it is a tree, it rolls up in every report, and it is worth designing before data arrives — with one extra power groups don't have: territories can carry targets.

Designing for Nigeria. The right granularity follows your commercial footprint, not the atlas. A Lagos-centric firm with national ambitions might use: All Territories → Lagos (→ Mainland · Island · Lagos West), South-West (ex-Lagos), Abuja & North-Central, South-East, South-South, North, Export (→ Ghana · Other West Africa). Twelve leaves. The tests: (1) every customer lands somewhere obvious; (2) each leaf is worth measuring on its own — if you'd never look at "North-East" alone, don't create it yet; split when the business arrives; (3) the top branches match how you'd staff regional responsibility, because territory performance and regional accountability should read off the same tree.

The two anti-patterns, again, with reasons. A territory named after a salesperson welds an org-chart snapshot into your geography: when Tunde resigns, "Tunde's Area" becomes archaeology, and reassigning his customers rewrites history's meaning. People belong in the Sales Person tree (Selling 8), which exists precisely so geography and staffing can change independently. And a territory set to a warehouse confuses where we sell with where we ship from — a Mainland customer served from an Island warehouse is still Mainland revenue.

Targets on territories. A territory can carry sales targets by item group and fiscal period. Set ₦120m for Lagos Mainland this year, and territory reports show actual against target with the tree rolling both up. This is the lightest-weight regional performance system you can run — no spreadsheets, no arguments about whose number is whose, because the number is computed from the same documents that raised the invoices.

Territory in the machinery. Like groups, territories serve as conditions: pricing rules can target them (a promo for South-East only), and analytics slice by them natively (Sales Analytics grouped by Territory is your regional revenue map, Selling 6). Export as a branch matters here: separating Ghana under Export keeps cross-border pricing rules and FX-flavoured analysis clean.

Assignment and hygiene. Every customer gets exactly one territory at creation (Chapter 1). For chains, the territory of the customer is where the relationship is managed — usually the head office — while individual branch geography lives on the shipping addresses (Chapter 5); don't fragment one chain across territories unless you genuinely manage the regions as separate relationships. Same weekly hygiene habit as groups: review new customers, catch misfiles early.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Contacts: the people layer
lessons.html:
A Customer is a company; you cannot phone a company. The people you actually deal with — the procurement officer, the pharmacist-owner, the accounts payable clerk — live as Contact records linked to the customer. Modelling them properly is the difference between institutional relationships and relationships that resign when one staff member (theirs or yours) does.

What a Contact carries. First and last name, designation ("Head of Procurement"), one or more email addresses, one or more phone numbers (each list with its own primary), and the link to the customer (a contact can even serve multiple parties — a consultant procuring for two sister companies). Create contacts from the customer's dashboard (the linked Contacts section) so the link is born correct, or from the Contact list directly.

The placement rule. When a buyer gives you a phone number, it goes on a Contact. Not appended to the customer name ("Alpha Pharmacy — call Ngozi 0803…" is a real record in many bad implementations), not buried in a quotation's remarks (unfindable in a month), not in a private phonebook (gone when your rep leaves). The Contact record is searchable, appears on documents, syncs to communications, and — critically — belongs to the company's relationship with the customer, not to any individual rep's.

Primary contact. Exactly one contact per customer should carry the primary flag. Documents pull the primary contact by default — not the newest contact, not the first alphabetically, not whoever was used last. So the operational meaning of "primary" is: who should a document address when nobody chooses? Usually the commercial decision-maker for quotations. You can always switch a given document to another of the customer's contacts; primary just sets the sane starting point.

Multiple contacts, deliberately. A healthy B2B customer record carries at least three people: the commercial contact (quotations, negotiations), the operational contact (deliveries — the store manager who receives goods), and the finance contact (invoices, statements, the person you chase at collections time, Selling 7). Capturing all three at onboarding costs five minutes and removes the single most common friction in fulfilment and collections: "who do we even talk to about this?"

Lifecycle. People move. When the procurement officer changes, you edit or replace the contact and re-flag primary — the customer, its history, its balances are untouched. That separation (company-level customer, person-level contacts) is exactly why the layer exists; firms that encode people into customer names get to rename their history every time someone resigns.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Addresses & the chain-modelling walkthrough
lessons.html:
Addresses answer where things happen: where invoices are addressed, where goods land. Like contacts they are separate records linked to the customer — one company, many places — and they carry the single most consequential modelling decision in Nigerian retail implementations: how to represent a chain.

What an Address carries. Title, address lines, city, state, country; a type — Billing, Shipping, or both; the link to its customer; and a primary flag per role. Create from the customer's dashboard so linkage is automatic.

Billing vs shipping. The billing address is the invoice's legal face — head office, where the TIN lives. Shipping addresses are delivery reality — stores, warehouses, branches. One customer routinely has one billing address and many shipping addresses, and documents let you pick: the invoice wears billing; each delivery note wears the branch it's actually going to.

Primary flags. As with contacts: documents pull the primary address by default. When a quotation shows the wrong address, the fix is almost always on the address records — the wrong one is flagged primary, or the right one was never created — not on the quotation. Diagnose at the master; the documents will follow.

THE CHAIN WALKTHROUGH. Your customer is a pharmacy chain: head office in Ikeja, 30 branches across Lagos and Ibadan, one procurement department, one account to settle. The correct model, end to end:

  1. One Customer record — "MediPlus Pharmacies Ltd". One, not thirty. The customer is the commercial relationship: one credit limit governing total exposure, one receivable balance, one statement, one negotiated price list, one history. Thirty customer records would shatter every one of those into thirty fragments — credit control becomes fiction (each "customer" under its limit while the chain owes triple your comfort), statements become a monthly reconciliation war, and "how much did MediPlus buy this year?" becomes a report nobody can run.
  2. One billing address — head office, primary billing. Every invoice addresses Ikeja, where accounts payable lives.
  3. Thirty shipping addresses — "MediPlus — Surulere", "MediPlus — Yaba", … "MediPlus — Bodija". Named so pickers and drivers recognise them instantly. Each delivery note selects its branch; the waybill prints the right street; and delivered-to history per branch is queryable forever.
  4. Contacts per role (Chapter 4) — procurement at HQ (primary), finance at HQ, and optionally key store managers attached as operational contacts.
  5. What NOT to do — addresses retyped per order (typos become failed deliveries and history becomes text nobody can group), or a hybrid "main branches as customers, small ones as addresses" (the worst of both: fragmented finance and inconsistent shipping data).

The exception that proves the rule. Model branches as separate customers only when they genuinely are separate commercial relationships — franchisees who buy and pay independently, each with its own credit standing. Then each franchisee IS a customer (perhaps grouped under a "MediPlus Franchise" customer group for rollup). The test is always: who owes the money? One payer, one customer.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Credit limits & the credit-control workflow
lessons.html:
Every credit sale is a loan wearing a delivery note. This chapter is the end-to-end workflow that keeps those loans deliberate: the limit, the block, the controller, and the review.

What the limit is — precisely. The Credit Limit, set in the customer's Credit Limits section (settable per company if you run several), caps the customer's unpaid outstanding exposure: their open invoices plus committed-but-unbilled orders, now. It is not lifetime purchases (a decade-old customer hasn't "used up" anything by volume), not a count of orders, and not a discount ceiling. Exposure — what you'd lose if they vanished tonight.

Setting the number. New customer, no history: start conservative — one typical order's value, or trade-reference-informed. Established customer: their payment behaviour is your underwriting; a customer who clears ₦8m monthly like clockwork can carry ₦10–15m. The limit is a policy dial, reviewed (see below), not a one-time guess.

The block. When a new Sales Order or invoice would push outstanding past the limit, ZhiftERP blocks submission with a credit-limit message. Understand the timing philosophically: the block fires at the moment of maximum temptation — the deal is closing, the rep wants the number, the customer is asking nicely. That is exactly when policy must be mechanical, because "just this once" evaluated by the person carrying the sales target is not evaluation.

The bypass — the Credit Controller. Exceptions must be possible (a strategic customer mid-payment-run deserves flexibility) but must be owned. Only a user holding the Credit Controller role can release a blocked document — per document, deliberately, their name on the action. Not any System Manager by default, not the salesperson who raised it, and not "nobody until they pay" (that's not a policy, it's an outage). Organisationally: give the role to finance, never to sales — the person who wants the deal must not be the person who waives the risk. In an 11-person firm that's the accountant or the MD; the point is the separation, not the headcount.

The bypass conversation, scripted. Rep hits the block → rep messages the controller with three facts: how much over, what's the customer's ageing (Selling 7's AR report), and when payment is expected → controller decides: release this document, raise the limit properly, or hold the order (Selling 4) until money lands. Sixty seconds, recorded in the system's own trail. What the workflow prevents is the alternative that kills firms slowly: goods shipping on charm while finance discovers the exposure at month-end.

The review cadence. Quarterly, run the AR ageing next to the limits: customers paying flawlessly at 80% utilisation are candidates for raises (don't strangle good growth); customers living in the 61-90 bucket get cuts or cash-only status. Limits that never move are limits nobody believes in.

The commercial truth to teach every rep: the difference between a sales team that grows revenue and one that grows bad debt is rarely closing skill — it is whether credit policy executes automatically at the point of entry or gets "reviewed" by humans after the goods have left. The block is not the system doubting you; it is the system doing the one job charm cannot.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Selling Settings for foundations
lessons.html:
Selling Settings (type it in the awesome bar) is one screen of switches where selling policy becomes system behaviour. Selling 8 walks every switch as the advanced treatment; a foundations trainee needs to command the following subset now, because they shape the documents you'll make from Chapter 1's customers.

Customer Naming By. Customer Name makes the typed name the record's permanent ID; Naming Series issues CUST-00042-style IDs with the name as display label. Preview of the Selling 8 decision rule: portfolios with duplicate or near-duplicate names — chains, common Nigerian trading names — need the series, because IDs must be unambiguous forever even when names aren't. What matters at foundations level: know that this is where record identity is decided, and that it's a day-one decision (changing naming schemes mid-life is migration surgery).

The defaults trio. Default Customer Group, default Territory, default Selling Price List. These pre-fill new customers and documents when nobody chooses. Set each to your genuinely commonest case — hurried data entry then lands correctly instead of blank. And connect this to Chapters 2–3's hygiene: defaults are a safety net, not a filing system; the weekly new-customer review catches what fell into the net.

Allow Item to be Added Multiple Times in a Transaction. Off: the same item cannot appear on two rows of one order (duplicate protection). On: it can — the legitimate case being the same item at two rates on one document, like 100 units at list plus 20 promotional units at zero, as two visible rows rather than a doctored average rate. This switch lives HERE — not on the item master, not on the price list, not in a print format — and knowing its address is a straight exam fact and a straight support fact.

Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle. The rate agreed on the Sales Order cannot silently differ on the Delivery Note or Sales Invoice made from it. What it defends against is precisely rate drift between the documents of one sale — the ₦850 the customer signed becoming ₦880 at invoice because someone "tidied" it. It is not currency management (Selling 2's conversion machinery), not discount control (Selling 6), not tax recalculation (templates). Its companion action setting — hard Stop versus Warning — is the Selling 8 discussion; foundations level: know the switch, know what drift means, know why a customer who signs one number and is billed another becomes a former customer.

The consultant's reflex to build now: when a client asks "can the system stop staff doing X?", open this screen before you say anything. Most selling-policy questions are already switches; the expensive consultant is the one who writes a customisation for a checkbox.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: onboarding a 30-branch pharmacy chain
lessons.html:
Theory becomes competence in the doing. This chapter onboards a realistic customer end-to-end using everything in this module. Read it actively — every step names the chapter that taught it.

The client. MediPlus Pharmacies Ltd: head office Ikeja, 30 branches (24 Lagos, 6 Ibadan), central procurement, central payment, negotiated distributor-grade pricing, requesting 45-day terms. Your firm has agreed to supply.

Step 1 — The customer record (Ch. 1). Selling > Customer > New. Name: MediPlus Pharmacies Ltd (their CAC name). Type: Company. Customer Group: Retail → Pharmacy — Chain (Ch. 2's tree earning its keep: chain pharmacies report separately from independents). Territory: Lagos → Mainland — the relationship is managed from Ikeja; branch geography will live on addresses, and we do NOT fragment one payer across territories (Ch. 3, Ch. 5). Default Currency: NGN. Default Price List: Distributor NGN — their negotiated tier, so every quotation prices correctly without anyone remembering the deal (Ch. 1; machinery in Selling 2). Tax ID: their TIN, captured now while onboarding goodwill is high.

Step 2 — Payment terms. They asked 45 days; management approved. Set default Payment Terms on the customer to the Net-45 template — every invoice will inherit it (Selling 7) and nobody improvises terms at billing time.

Step 3 — Contacts (Ch. 4). Three people, created from the customer's dashboard: Ngozi E., Head of Procurement — primary (quotations address her); Ibrahim S., Accounts Payable (statements and collections address him — future-you at Selling 7 says thanks); Kemi A., Regional Ops (delivery escalations). Five minutes now; the "who do we even call?" friction never exists.

Step 4 — Addresses (Ch. 5). One billing address: head office, Ikeja — primary billing; every invoice wears it. Thirty shipping addresses, one per branch, named for humans: "MediPlus — Surulere", … "MediPlus — Bodija". (Thirty entries is an import job, not an afternoon of typing — the same import discipline Selling 2 teaches for prices.) Flag the highest-volume branch primary shipping; every delivery note picks its actual branch.

Step 5 — Credit (Ch. 6). Projected offtake ₦6m/month on 45-day terms means roughly two months' exposure in steady state: recommend a ₦15m limit, approved by finance, entered on the customer. Confirm the Credit Controller role sits with the accountant, not the sales lead. Diarise the first review for the end of quarter one: their actual payment behaviour will tell you whether ₦15m was generous or tight.

Step 6 — Verify the defaults end-to-end. Raise a draft test quotation for MediPlus (delete after): price list shows Distributor NGN ✓; currency NGN ✓; contact Ngozi ✓; billing address Ikeja ✓; a delivery-note address picker shows all thirty branches ✓. Ten minutes of verification beats a first live order that ships to the wrong city at retail rates.

Step 7 — The one-paragraph handover. In the client room / CRM: "MediPlus configured: 1 customer, 30 shipping addresses (import file attached), Distributor NGN pricing, Net-45, ₦15m limit (review 30 Sept), contacts: Ngozi (commercial), Ibrahim (finance), Kemi (ops)." The next consultant — or you in six months — reconstructs the whole setup from four lines.

What this setup buys, permanently: one statement Ibrahim can reconcile; one limit that actually caps the chain; branch-level delivery history; segment-true reporting (Pharmacy—Chain, Lagos Mainland); pricing that defaults right on every future document. Total work: under two hours, most of it the address import. Every hour skipped here is repaid weekly, with interest, forever.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & support patterns
lessons.html:
Every implementation team accumulates the same scar tissue. This chapter hands you the scars pre-earned: the foundations mistakes you will meet in the field, how they present as support tickets, and the fixes — so you recognise the disease from the symptom in one move.

Pattern 1 — "The quotation shows the wrong address/contact." Disease: primary flags (Ch. 4-5) — the wrong record is flagged primary, or the right record was never created and the only one wins by default. Fix at the master: create/flag correctly; the documents follow. Anti-fix: editing the document, which cures one quotation and leaves every future one wrong.

Pattern 2 — "Wrong currency/prices keep appearing for this customer." Disease: Default Currency or Default Price List on the master (Ch. 1). The document is faithfully inheriting a wrong default. Fix the field; stop treating documents.

Pattern 3 — "We can't tell how much the chain owes us" / statements chaos. Disease: the chain was modelled as many customers (Ch. 5's cardinal sin). Each fragment is individually under-limit and individually statement-ed while the real payer's exposure is invisible. Fix: consolidate to one customer with shipping addresses — a data-migration exercise (re-pointing open documents and balances) that gets harder every month it waits, which is why the walkthrough exists.

Pattern 4 — "Reports say most of our sales are in 'All Customer Groups'." Disease: creation-time laziness plus a root-level default (Ch. 2, Ch. 7). Everyone was filed in the landfill. Fix forward: set a real default leaf, institute the weekly new-customer review. Fix backward: a one-time regrouping exercise — tedious, and the reports only speak from the day assignments are true.

Pattern 5 — "Sales by region is meaningless / territories named after ex-staff." Disease: people encoded into geography (Ch. 3). Fix: rebuild territories as geography, move staffing to the Sales Person tree (Selling 8), reassign customers once.

Pattern 6 — "The system blocked my order and the client is waiting!" Not a disease — the credit block working (Ch. 6). The support answer is the workflow, not a workaround: check exposure and ageing, route to the Credit Controller, release / raise / hold deliberately. The ticket to ESCALATE is its inverse: "can you give my user the bypass so this stops happening" — that's a request to disable credit control, and it goes to management, not to a permissions tweak.

Pattern 7 — "Duplicate customers everywhere." Disease: name-based creation without discipline ("Alpha Pharmacy", "Alpha Pharmacy Ltd", "ALPHA PHARM") — each with partial history. Prevention: naming-series IDs (Ch. 7 / Selling 8) plus a search-before-create habit. Cure: merge/re-point, then prevention — duplicates recreate themselves wherever the habit that made them survives.

The meta-pattern. Read the seven again: every single one is a master-data disease presenting as a document symptom. That is the deepest lesson of this module — documents are downstream of masters. The consultant who fixes masters closes tickets permanently; the one who fixes documents subscribes to them. When a selling support ticket arrives, your first question is now reflex: which master record is lying?

questions.q: Which three Customer fields most directly drive sales reporting in ZhiftERP?
opts: Customer Group, Territory, and the customer name
questions.why: Group and territory are the analysis dimensions every sales report slices by.

questions.q: A customer's quotations keep defaulting to the wrong currency. Where is the durable fix?
questions.why: Document defaults flow from the customer master — fix the master, not the symptom.

questions.q: One customer with 30 branches needing deliveries to each branch is modelled as:
opts: One customer, addresses typed per order
questions.why: One company = one customer; locations are address records attached to it.

questions.q: Documents pull which contact and address by default?
opts: The primary contact and primary address
questions.why: The primary flags control defaulting.

questions.q: A Sales Order is blocked because the customer would exceed their credit limit. Who can let it through?
opts: A user with the Credit Controller role
The sales user who made it
Nobody — it must be paid first
questions.why: Credit Controller is the deliberate bypass role for credit-limit blocks.

questions.q: The credit limit measures the customer's:
questions.why: It caps outstanding receivables, not sales volume.

questions.q: Where do you control whether the same item can appear on two rows of one order?
opts: Selling Settings — Allow Item to be Added Multiple Times
questions.why: It's a Selling Settings switch.

questions.q: "Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle" protects against:
opts: The rate silently differing between order and delivery/invoice
questions.why: It enforces the agreed rate downstream through the cycle.

questions.q: Customer Group answers which question about a customer?
opts: What kind of customer they are
questions.why: Group is the kind/segment dimension; territory is the where.

questions.q: The right place to record a buyer's phone number is:
opts: A Contact linked to the customer
questions.why: People live on Contact records, linked to the customer.

questions.q: Territory on the customer is best set to:
opts: The geographic region used in your reporting structure
questions.why: Territory is the geography dimension for analysis and targets.

questions.q: A new customer record should always be created with:
opts: A copied address from another customer
Name, group, territory, currency and default price list set deliberately
questions.why: Master data created deliberately keeps every later document and report clean.

questions.q: At onboarding, when is the right moment to capture a company customer's TIN?
opts: At onboarding, while goodwill is high
questions.why: Chasing TINs at invoice time stalls billing; capture at creation.

questions.q: A healthy B2B customer record carries at least which three contacts?
questions.why: Quotations, deliveries, and collections each need a named person.

questions.q: The customer's territory for a 30-branch chain managed from head office should be:
opts: The head office's territory, with branch geography on shipping addresses
questions.why: One relationship, one territory; branch geography lives on addresses.

questions.q: Franchise branches that buy and pay independently should be modelled as:
opts: Separate customers — the test is who owes the money
questions.why: Independent payers are independent commercial relationships.

questions.q: What makes 'Default Customer Group' safe rather than a landfill?
opts: A real common leaf plus a weekly review of newly created customers
Pointing it at the root group
questions.why: Defaults are a safety net; the review catches misfiles young.

questions.q: Credit limits should be reviewed:
opts: On a cadence (e.g. quarterly) against AR ageing
questions.why: Flawless payers at high utilisation get raises; 61-90 dwellers get cuts.

questions.q: A rep hits the credit block. Per the workflow, the message to the controller carries:
opts: Amount over, the customer's ageing, expected payment date
questions.why: Three facts let the controller decide in sixty seconds.

questions.q: A support user asks you to grant their login the credit bypass 'so this stops happening'. You:
opts: Escalate to management — it's a request to disable credit control
questions.why: Permanent bypass for sales is credit control switched off.

questions.q: MediPlus's 30 branch addresses are best entered by:
opts: A data import of the address file
One address reused with edits per order
questions.why: Thirty structured records is an import job, not an afternoon of typing.

questions.q: Reports show most sales under 'All Customer Groups'. The backward fix is:
opts: A one-time regrouping exercise; reports speak from when assignments are true
questions.why: Forward hygiene plus one cleanup; unassigned history stays unsegmentable until regrouped.

questions.q: The deepest law of foundations support is:
opts: Documents are downstream of masters — find the lying master
questions.why: Every recurring document symptom traces to a master-data disease.

questions.q: Why must the Credit Controller role sit in finance rather than sales?
opts: The person who wants the deal must not be the one who waives the risk
questions.why: Separation of desire and approval is the point of the role.

questions.q: Verifying a new customer setup end-to-end is best done by:

items_prices.title: Selling 2 — Items & Price Lists
items_prices.desc: Sellable items, units of measure, selling price lists and Item Prices — where every rate on every quotation actually comes from.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Item master for selling, field by field
lessons.html:
If the customer master answers who, the item master answers what — and just as in Selling 1, the quality of the master decides the quality of every document that touches it. This chapter walks the item record through a seller's eyes: which fields make an item sellable, findable, priceable, and reportable.

The gate: Is Sales Item. One checkbox decides whether an item can appear on selling documents at all. Ticked, the item is offered on quotations, orders, delivery notes, invoices; unticked, it is invisible to the selling side no matter how much stock exists. This is deliberate: purchase-only components, internal consumables, packaging materials, and fixed assets live in the same item table but must never be quotable. The support reflex this creates — and it is the FIRST check, before price, before customer, before warehouse — is: "an item refuses to appear on a quotation" → open the item → is Is Sales Item ticked? Thirty seconds; ticket closed.

Item Code and Item Name. The code is the permanent identity — short, unique, never recycled, never changed once transactions exist (a changed code orphans history). The name is the human label that prints on documents. Discipline for codes in Nigerian retail practice: a scheme the warehouse can read (PARA-500-TAB tells a picker more than ITM-0042), agreed once, enforced always. Duplicate items — the same product created twice under slightly different names — are the item-side twin of Selling 1's duplicate customers, and Chapter 9 treats the cure; here, build the habit: search before you create.

Item Group. The reporting dimension. It serves for items exactly what Customer Group serves for customers: the segment/rollup axis every sales report slices by — Beverages, Antibiotics, Hardware, Services. It is a tree, designed (Chapter 3), not accreted. Note the symmetry consciously, because exam questions and client conversations both lean on it: customer group answers what kind of buyer; item group answers what kind of product; territory answers where — the three axes of every serious sales analysis.

Description. What prints on documents beneath the name. Write it for the customer's eyes — spec, pack size, grade — because this text IS your quotation line. A blank description on a ₦5m line item reads as carelessness to the buyer's procurement office.

Maintain Stock. Ticked for physical goods (the system tracks quantity); unticked for services and for bundle parents (Selling 8's Product Bundles). A consulting-fee item with Maintain Stock ticked will one day block an invoice for "insufficient stock" of something that never existed — a classic mis-setup found in the wild.

Flags that matter later. Has Serial No and Has Batch No switch on per-unit and per-lot identity — their operational weight lands at delivery time (Selling 5: exact serials on the DN, recall-by-batch), but they are set here, at item creation, and retro-fitting them after transactions exist is painful. Pharma and electronics implementations decide these flags on day one.

Standard Selling Rate. A convenience field used when no Item Price exists — a fallback, not the pricing system. Real rates live in Item Price records against price lists (Chapters 4-5); treat this field as scaffolding for brand-new setups, not as where pricing happens.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Units of Measure: the carton walkthrough
lessons.html:
Nigerian trade sells in cartons, packs, dozens, bundles, jerrycans — and counts stock in pieces. The UOM machinery is how one item lives honestly in both worlds, and getting it wrong double-counts or twelfth-counts stock with real money attached. This chapter makes the arithmetic reflexive.

Default Unit of Measure — the counting unit. The item's Default UOM is the unit stock is kept and counted in — the stock-keeping unit. If the warehouse counts pieces, Default UOM is Unit (Nos), full stop. Every stock report, every valuation, every bin quantity speaks this unit. It is not the carton size, not the price-list unit, not the selling unit — it is the physical count language of the warehouse, chosen once and never casually changed (a changed default UOM re-denominates history).

Sales UOM — the selling unit. When you sell in a different unit than you count, set the Sales UOM. Stock in Units, sell in Cartons: Sales UOM = Carton. Selling documents then default to cartons for this item, which is how the trade actually talks.

The conversion factor — where the arithmetic lives. In the item's UOM table, add the row: Carton, conversion factor 12 (one carton = twelve stock units). Now the system does the arithmetic everywhere, forever: a quotation for 5 Cartons prices 5 × the carton rate, and its delivery deducts 60 Units from stock. One item record, two honest languages.

The wrong answers, and why they fail. (1) Two item records — "Paracetamol (Unit)" and "Paracetamol (Carton)" — splits one physical stock into two ledgers that instantly disagree: sell a carton and the unit item's stock doesn't move; every stocktake becomes a reconciliation between two records of the same shelf. (2) Manual arithmetic on rows — "just type 60 units when they order 5 cartons" — survives until the first tired Friday, when 6 cartons ships as 6 units and a customer receives a twelfth of their order. The conversion factor exists so no human does trade arithmetic under deadline.

Multiple UOMs. The table holds as many as trade needs: Unit (factor 1, the default), Pack of 4 (factor 4), Carton (factor 12), Pallet (factor 288). Documents can transact any of them; stock always resolves to the default UOM underneath.

Pricing meets UOM — a preview with teeth. Item Prices (Chapter 5) are stated against a UOM. Price the Carton at ₦10,200 for carton-trade lists; the unit-retail list prices the Unit at ₦1,000. Keep list, UOM, and rate coherent — the classic field bug is a carton rate sitting on a unit row (an order of "5" priced as 5 cartons but understood by the warehouse as 5 units), and Chapter 9 shows how that ticket presents. The prevention is discipline you now have: every rate knows its unit.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Item Groups: designing the product tree
lessons.html:
Selling 1 Chapter 2 taught segmentation-tree design for customers; this chapter is its mirror for products, shorter because the design logic transfers — and it should transfer consciously, since the symmetry itself is the lesson.

The mechanics. Item Groups form a tree (group nodes and leaves); items attach to leaves; reports roll leaves up through parents. "Analgesics" and "Antibiotics" sum into "Pharma", which sums into the root. Sales Analytics grouped by Item Group is your product-mix instrument (Selling 6), and the tree you design here is the shape of every answer it will ever give.

The three rules, transferred. (1) One question per tree — item group answers what kind of product. Do not encode supplier (that's the buying side), location (warehouses), or price tier (price lists) into group names. (2) Mirror management's language — if the MD asks "how did Pharma do against FMCG?", those are the top branches. (3) Two-second leaves — every item obviously belongs somewhere; if creation-time filing needs a debate, the tree is too clever. Ten to twenty leaves serves most mid-market catalogs.

A worked tree for a dual-channel distributor: All Item Groups → Pharma (→ Analgesics · Antibiotics · Supplements), FMCG (→ Beverages · Personal Care · Home Care), Equipment (→ Retail Hardware · Spare Parts), Services (→ Installation · Support Plans). Note Services as a first-class branch: service items (Maintain Stock off, Chapter 1) deserve reporting identity too — firms that dump services into "Misc" cannot answer "how much of our revenue is recurring service?", which is exactly the question a SaaS-minded MD asks.

Groups as machinery. As with customers, the group is a condition elsewhere: pricing rules target item groups ("10% off all Beverages in Q4", Selling 6), and sales-person targets are set per item group (Selling 8). A clean tree makes policy aimable; a mushy one makes every rule a special case.

Hygiene. Same habits as Selling 1: a real default leaf in settings rather than a landfill, search-before-create, and a periodic review of recently created items. Re-parenting is cheap and takes effect in reports immediately; history filed into "All Item Groups" for a year is unsegmentable forever.

Two adjacent fields, placed correctly. Brand is its own field on the item — Coca-Cola vs Rite Foods across the Beverages leaf — so brand analysis never needs brand-flavoured group names; keep brand out of the tree and in its field. And item variants (one template, many size/colour children) are the machinery for true variations of one product — a polo shirt in five sizes is one template with variants, not five leaves and not five unrelated items; if you find yourself designing group leaves per size, the variant system is what you actually wanted. Both belong to deeper item-master work, but knowing they exist stops the tree absorbing jobs that aren't its.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Price Lists: the architecture of who pays what
lessons.html:
A Price List is a named collection of selling rates in exactly one currency — and that constraint is structural: the list IS a currency context, not a folder with a currency sticker. This chapter is about using lists as what they really are: the architecture of your commercial arrangements.

The defaulting chain — machinery you must recite cold. Every selling document carries a price list field. The list lands there from the customer's Default Price List (Selling 1 Chapter 1); if the customer has none, the global default from Selling Settings applies. Each document row's rate is then looked up from that document's list in the Item Price table (Chapter 5). Customer → document → row: three links, and every pricing support ticket is a break in one of them.

Lists over discounts — the design principle with the reasons attached. Retail pays ₦1,000; distributors pay ₦850. The clean model is two lists — Standard Selling and Distributor NGN — each with its own Item Price. The rejected alternatives, and why:

  • A 15% distributor discount — now every report shows ₦1,000 minus noise; margin analysis must mentally un-discount every row; "discount" as a word stops meaning anything exceptional; and the day you reprice retail, the distributor price moves too, whether you meant it or not. Coupled prices are accidental prices.
  • Two item records — Chapter 2 already convicted this: one product, two stock ledgers.
  • Manual rate edits per document — pricing by memory, enforced by nobody, invisible to every report.

With separate lists, each channel's report shows its true agreed rate, each reprices independently, and discounts (Selling 6) are reserved for genuine exceptions — which keeps them visible, which keeps them controllable.

How many lists? One per commercial arrangement per currency: Standard Selling (NGN retail), Distributor NGN, Key Accounts NGN (if negotiated tiers truly differ), Export USD. Four or five lists is architecture; fifteen is pricing chaos wearing a filing system — at that point the real structure you need is pricing rules over fewer lists.

Selling vs buying lists. The same Price List doctype serves both sides, distinguished by its Selling / Buying checkboxes. A consultant never confuses which side a list feeds; the checkbox says. (Your purchase-cost story lives in the Buying track.)

Enabled/disabled. Lists can be disabled — the right end for a retired arrangement, preserving history without offering the list on new documents. Deleting a list with history is the wrong end.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Item Price records & the rate-0 clinic
lessons.html:
The price list is the folder; the Item Price is the atom: one item + one price list + one rate, optionally scoped. ₦1,000 for PARA-500 on Standard Selling is one record. Everything a document charges traces to one of these atoms — which is why the most common selling support ticket in existence resolves here.

The clinic: "why is my rate 0?" A quotation row shows rate 0.00. The overwhelming cause: no Item Price exists for that item on the document's price list. The document asked its list; the list had no row for the item; zero came back — not an error, an honest empty answer. The diagnostic sequence, in order: (1) what price list is on the document? (2) does an Item Price exist for this item on that list? (3) if scoped — is today inside its validity window, and does the row's quantity meet its minimum? Ninety percent of tickets end at step 2 with a missing record; the rest at step 3 with an expired promo or an unmet min-qty. What the cause is NOT: the item being inactive (inactive items don't appear at all — Chapter 1), taxes (they compute after the rate), or the customer's territory (a reporting dimension, not a pricing input).

Scoping an Item Price. Two optional fields turn a flat rate into a policy: valid from / valid upto dates — a September promo rate that starts and expires itself, no memo, no cleanup — and minimum quantity — ₦950 from 50 units up, coexisting with the standard ₦1,000 row; the document picks by quantity. These two, and only these two, are how an Item Price is scoped: not by warehouse, not by salesperson, not by payment terms (those concerns belong to other machinery entirely — pricing rules, sales-person assignment, terms templates).

UOM on the price. From Chapter 2: every rate knows its unit. The carton rate is stated against the Carton UOM; the unit rate against Unit. A rate on the wrong UOM row is the silent 12× error, and Chapter 9 shows its ticket face.

Where rates come from — the recitation. A document row's rate comes from the Item Price for the document's price list — not from the item's standard rate whenever a real Item Price exists (that field is fallback scaffolding, Chapter 1), not from the last invoice (there is no "price memory" between documents), not from Selling Settings. Say it until it's reflex, because half of pricing support is repeating this sentence with the screen open.

Coexisting rows, resolved. When several Item Prices legitimately coexist for one item on one list — standard ₦1,000; promo ₦950 min-qty 50, dated — the document resolves by scope: quantity meets the minimum and today sits in the window → the scoped row wins; otherwise the standard row. And on the document itself notice the two fields per row: Price List Rate (what the lookup returned — the list's truth) and Rate (what this document charges). They start equal; a negotiated override changes Rate while Price List Rate stands as the reference — which is exactly how override reporting (Selling 3) can compare charged against list without archaeology.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Bulk price maintenance: the import workflow
lessons.html:
Quarter-start. Costs moved, FX moved, and 300 selling rates must change by Monday. This chapter is the workflow that does it in an hour without a single typo becoming an invoice.

The principle: bulk price maintenance is an import job. The cycle: export → edit in the sheet → re-import. Concretely: from the Item Price list, filter to the target price list, export via the data-export tool including the record IDs; open the sheet; update the rate column (this is where spreadsheet skill earns money — a formula applying +8% to a cost-driven subset beats 300 manual edits); re-import in update mode, matching on ID so each existing record is amended in place.

Why not the alternatives. Editing each Item Price by hand — 300 open-edit-save cycles at human error rates; the one typo (₦10,200 entered as ₦1,020) ships on a real order before anyone notices. Deleting the list and rebuilding — history evaporates, scoped promo rows die with it, and for the rebuild window the list is empty: every document raised meanwhile prices at 0 (Chapter 5's clinic, self-inflicted, fleet-wide). Patching with pricing rules — a rule stacking +8% on stale base rates buries the true price under arithmetic; rules are for conditional policy (Selling 6), not for deferred maintenance of base rates.

The safety habits. Export a backup copy of the list before editing (the rollback is then itself a one-import job). Spot-check ten rows after import against the sheet. Announce the effective date to the sales floor — quotations already in Draft keep their fetched rates until refreshed, and reps should know which world they're quoting in.

Validity-dated repricing — the elegant variant. For a planned future change, import the new rates as additional Item Price rows with valid from = the effective date, and set valid upto on the old rows to the day before. The price change then executes itself at midnight, atomically, with zero downtime and a perfect audit trail of what was charged when — the professional's version of "remember to update prices on the 1st".

Cadence. In an FX-exposed market, price review is a rhythm, not an event: a monthly thirty-minute review of cost-driven lists (with Chapter 7's currency machinery absorbing pure FX drift on export lists) keeps repricing boring — and boring is the goal.

Who owns repricing. Give bulk price maintenance a named owner and a change log kept as the export files themselves — dated backup exports ARE the price history, reconstructible to any Monday. And pair the workflow with the Chapter 4 permission stance: with Allow-User-to-Edit-Price-List-Rate off for the sales floor (Selling 8), the import workflow is the ONLY door prices move through — one owner, one method, one trail. Firms that can answer "who changed this rate, when, from what to what?" in one minute are firms whose margins survive audits and arguments alike.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Multi-currency pricing
lessons.html:
One list, one currency — so what happens when currencies meet? This chapter is the machinery and the architecture for pricing across the naira boundary.

The mechanics. A USD price list is selected (or defaults) onto a document whose currency is NGN. The result is: not an error, not zero rates, not dollars printing on a naira invoice — ZhiftERP converts automatically, using the Currency Exchange rate, into the document's currency, and the document displays the conversion rate it used. The customer sees naira; the list stays dollars; the bridge is explicit and auditable on the document itself.

Where rates come from. Currency Exchange records hold the rates, datestamped, and can auto-fetch daily from providers. For manual regimes (or CBN-vs-parallel realities), rates can be entered deliberately — and a document can carry an overridden conversion rate when a deal was struck at an agreed rate. The audit principle: every converted amount traces to a visible rate on the document.

The architecture win — import-priced goods. Electronics, equipment, anything dollar-costed: hold the stable dollar price on the USD list and let conversion happen per document at the current rate. Your naira quotations then track FX automatically — no human reprices anything when the rate moves. The rejected alternative — maintaining a naira copy of dollar prices — goes stale the day the rate moves and turns every FX swing into Chapter 6's bulk-import job. One source of truth per price; conversion is computation, not maintenance.

The structuring rule, restated with currency. One price list per currency per commercial arrangement: Distributor USD for the Ghana channel, Export USD for other West Africa, Standard Selling in NGN — and the customer's default does the choosing (Selling 1): the Accra distributor's master points at Distributor USD; the Surulere pharmacy at Standard Selling; nobody picks lists at quotation time and nobody quotes the wrong currency by accident.

The boundary of this module. Multi-currency also touches the receivable's currency, exchange-gain/loss on settlement, and revaluation — accounting depths that belong to the Accounts track. A Sales Professional owns everything above: the pricing mechanics, the conversion trail on documents, and the architecture that keeps FX a computation instead of a monthly emergency.

Two field realities to handle gracefully. First, agreed-rate deals: an export order struck at a locked ₦/$ rate carries that rate as the document's conversion override — deliberate, visible, and better than editing prices to fake it; the list stays pure, the deal stays honest. Second, rounding: converted amounts produce kobo-level fractions; currency precision settings and the invoice's rounding row absorb them so totals stay payable — never hand-round a converted rate on the row, because the payment allocation (Selling 7) must later match the document to the kobo.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: pricing architecture for a dual-channel vendor
lessons.html:
Everything in this module, executed once, end to end. The client is your own commercial reality in miniature; every step names its chapter.

The business. HealthTrade Ltd sells pharmacy consumables two ways: retail counters buy by the unit at list; distributors buy by the carton (12s) at trade rates; and a Ghana distributor buys the same cartons priced in USD. A Q4 promo is planned: units at ₦950 from 50 units up, September–November. Build the whole pricing architecture.

Step 1 — The item, once (Ch. 1-2). Item PARA-500, "Paracetamol 500mg Tablets", Is Sales Item ✓, Maintain Stock ✓, Item Group Pharma → Analgesics (Ch. 3's tree). Default UOM: Unit — the warehouse counts pieces. UOM table: add Carton, factor 12. One item record; both trade languages; the conversion factor owns the arithmetic forever. (Two item records was rejected in Chapter 2 and stays rejected.)

Step 2 — The lists (Ch. 4). Three, one per arrangement per currency: Standard Selling (NGN — exists), Distributor NGN, Distributor USD. Not a "distributor discount" on the retail list — separate lists so each channel reports its true rate and reprices independently.

Step 3 — The Item Prices (Ch. 5). Four atoms: PARA-500 · Standard Selling · Unit · ₦1,000. PARA-500 · Distributor NGN · Carton · ₦10,200. PARA-500 · Distributor USD · Carton · $6.80. And the promo: PARA-500 · Standard Selling · Unit · ₦950, min qty 50, valid 01-Sep → 30-Nov — it will switch itself on, apply itself only to qualifying quantities, and expire itself, no memo ever written (Ch. 5-6). Note every rate declaring its UOM — the carton rate on the Carton row, the silent-12×-error made impossible.

Step 4 — Customers choose lists by default (Ch. 4; Selling 1). Retail customers' masters: Standard Selling. Nigerian distributors: Distributor NGN. The Accra distributor: Distributor USD, currency USD on their master. From this moment, every quotation for every channel prices itself correctly with nobody choosing anything.

Step 5 — Verify end-to-end. Draft quotations, one per channel (delete after): retail 60 units → ₦950 rate fires (min qty met, in window) ✓; retail 20 units → ₦1,000 ✓; distributor 5 Cartons → ₦10,200/carton, and the stock projection shows 60 Units committed ✓ (Ch. 2's arithmetic, working); Accra 5 Cartons on an NGN document → converted at today's Currency Exchange rate, rate visible on the document ✓ (Ch. 7).

Step 6 — The maintenance plan (Ch. 6-7). Distributor NGN reprices via export-edit-reimport when costs move, with validity-dated rows for planned changes; Distributor USD never chases FX — conversion does; the promo needs no cleanup — it dies on schedule. Handover note, four lines, filed in the client room.

What the architecture buys: three channels, two currencies, one item, one stock ledger, self-managing promos, FX absorbed by computation — and every report showing true agreed rates per channel. Total build: under an hour. The firms that skip it spend that hour weekly, in support tickets, forever.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & support patterns
lessons.html:
The scar tissue chapter for items and pricing: the tickets you will actually receive, the disease behind each, and the fix — plus the meta-pattern that by now you can predict.

Pattern 1 — "Item doesn't appear on the quotation." Disease: Is Sales Item unticked (Ch. 1). The first check, always. Runner-up disease: the item is disabled entirely. What it is not: pricing (an unpriced item appears at rate 0; a non-sales item doesn't appear at all — the symptom distinguishes the diseases).

Pattern 2 — "Rate shows 0." The clinic (Ch. 5): no Item Price for the item on the document's price list — or a scoped one whose window/min-qty doesn't match. Run the three-step diagnostic; fix the atom, not the document. Typing the rate onto the quotation "just this once" closes today's ticket and books tomorrow's — the next document asks the same empty list.

Pattern 3 — "Customer was quoted 12× too much / warehouse shipped a twelfth of the order." Disease: UOM incoherence (Ch. 2, 5) — a carton rate on a Unit row, or an order taken in the wrong UOM. Fix: correct the Item Price's UOM, verify the item's conversion table, re-issue the document. Prevention is the discipline: every rate knows its unit, checked at entry.

Pattern 4 — "Distributor prices moved when we repriced retail." Disease: channels coupled by a discount instead of separated by lists (Ch. 4). The %-off-retail "distributor pricing" faithfully tracked a retail change nobody meant to pass through. Fix: build the second list, migrate customers' defaults to it, retire the discount — decoupled channels reprice independently by construction.

Pattern 5 — "Half the catalog priced at 0 since Tuesday." Disease: a list rebuild done by delete-and-recreate, or an import that created new rows instead of updating existing ones, leaving the live list orphaned (Ch. 6). Fix: restore from the pre-edit export (you kept one — the workflow said so) and redo the import in update mode, matched on ID.

Pattern 6 — "The Ghana invoice used a strange exchange rate." Disease: a stale or manually mistyped Currency Exchange record, or a forgotten per-document override (Ch. 7). The document displays the rate it used — read it there first; the audit trail is on the page. Fix the exchange record or the override; re-issue if the deal rate was agreed differently.

Pattern 7 — "Same product exists three times." Disease: creation without search — PARA-500, "Paracetamol 500", "Panadol tabs (white box)" — each with partial stock and partial history (Ch. 1). Cure: pick the survivor, re-point and merge, retire the duplicates; then prevention — code discipline and search-before-create — because duplicates regrow wherever the habit that made them survives.

The meta-pattern, confirmed. Seven tickets; seven master-data diseases wearing document symptoms — the same law Selling 1 closed on: documents are downstream of masters. On the selling side the masters are two: who (customer, Selling 1) and what + at what rate (item and Item Price, this module). Command both and the document layer — quotations onward, starting next module — becomes almost boring. That is the goal. Boring documents are correct documents.

quotations.title: Selling 3 — Quotations
quotations.desc: The offer document: creating quotations, validity, taxes on the offer, the status lifecycle, losing gracefully, and converting to an order.

lessons.title: Creating the offer
lessons.html:
The Quotation is the first formal document of the cycle — the written offer. It can be made against an existing Customer or against a Lead (someone not yet a customer) — that flexibility matters: you don't create a customer master just to price an enquiry. Create from Selling > Quotation > New, or from a CRM opportunity so the trail from first contact to offer stays linked.

What you fill:

  • Party — the customer or lead. Their price list, currency, contact and address default in.
  • Items — code, quantity; the rate arrives from the price list automatically per the previous module.
  • Rate overrides — you MAY type over a price-list rate on any row. This is allowed, visible, and reportable — not forbidden, not manager-only, not automatic. The philosophy: empower the negotiation, but leave fingerprints. Reports can always compare charged rate vs list rate.
  • Valid Till — how long the offer stands. After this date the quotation automatically shows Expired. Fill it always: open-ended offers are how last year's prices get accepted this year.
  • Payment terms, terms & conditions — the commercial fine print that will travel forward.

Save produces a Draft you can still edit; Submit makes it a formal, numbered offer and moves it to Open. Print formats give it your letterhead for the customer's inbox.

lessons.title: Taxes on the quotation
lessons.html:
Quote taxes ON the offer — this is both mechanics and commercial judgment.

Mechanics: attach a Sales Taxes and Charges Template to the quotation — for Nigerian trade typically VAT at 7.5% — and the document computes and displays the tax rows and the grand total. VAT is never typed into item rates by hand and never derived from the customer group; the template row (account head + 7.5%) does it uniformly. Building the templates is covered deeply in Selling 6; here you need to know that one is selected on the document and does the work.

Commercial judgment: the reason to quote taxes is that the customer sees the true payable total from the first document. Quote ₦10m clean, invoice ₦10.75m later, and you have manufactured a dispute at the worst possible moment — after commitment, before payment. It is not a legal requirement on quotations that drives this; it is deal hygiene. No late surprises.

The template travels: the taxes chosen on the quotation flow onto the Sales Order made from it, and onward to delivery and invoice. Nobody re-enters taxes at each stage, and the offer's arithmetic is the invoice's arithmetic.

lessons.title: The status lifecycle
lessons.html:
A quotation's status is one word telling you exactly where the deal stands. Learn the vocabulary cold:

  • Draft — being written; editable; not yet an offer.
  • Open — submitted and awaiting the customer's answer. THE working state.
  • Ordered — won: a Sales Order has been made from it.
  • Lost — conceded, with a reason recorded.
  • Expired — Valid Till passed with no order; automatic.
  • Cancelled — withdrawn by you.

The operational habit: the Quotation list filtered to Open IS your offers-awaiting-answer pipeline — not Draft (those aren't offers yet), not All (that's history). A sales professional works that filter weekly: chase the old ones, expire-and-refresh the stale ones, mark the dead ones Lost honestly. An Open list you can trust is worth more than any forecast, because it's not a forecast — it's the actual set of live offers.

lessons.title: Losing well & converting
lessons.html:
Losing well: when a deal dies, mark the quotation Lost — and ZhiftERP prompts for a Lost Reason: price, competitor, timing, no budget, spec mismatch. Recording it costs ten seconds. Six months of honest lost reasons is a strategy document nobody had to write: if "price" dominates in one segment, your list rates are wrong there; if one competitor's name keeps appearing, you know exactly who to build battle-cards against. Lost reasons are competitive and pricing intelligence — not a blame record for reps, not noise, not a deletion queue. Teams that fake them (everything is "timing") throw the intelligence away.

Winning: when the customer says yes, do NOT open a blank Sales Order and retype. From the quotation: Create > Sales Order. Everything carries across — items, quantities, rates (including your negotiated overrides), taxes, terms — with no transcription errors, and the quotation flips to Ordered, closing the loop. The point of document flow is that the offer the customer accepted is BYTE-FOR-BYTE the order you fulfil; the moment someone retypes, the agreed deal and the recorded deal can diverge, and every dispute that follows is your fault.

This create-from-the-previous-document pattern is the spine of the whole cycle: quotation → order → delivery note → invoice, each born from its parent, nothing retyped, the chain of custody unbroken.

sales_orders.title: Selling 4 — Sales Orders
sales_orders.desc: The commitment document: delivery dates, what submission reserves, the status language, amendments, holds and closes, and delivery tolerance.

lessons.title: The commitment
lessons.html:
The Sales Order is where an offer becomes an obligation. The customer has said yes; you now owe specific goods at specific rates by a specific Delivery Date — and the business plans around that promise: stock gets reserved, procurement sees demand, the warehouse sees a pipeline of picks.

Preferred origin: created FROM the accepted quotation (Create > Sales Order), inheriting everything — the previous module explained why retyping is malpractice. Direct entry exists for genuinely quotation-less sales (repeat standing orders, counter trade), but "direct entry always" is the mark of a team not using the system's spine.

Delivery dates, properly: the order carries a header delivery date, and each row can carry its OWN — because real orders split: the shelving ships Monday, the imported scanners in three weeks. Per-row delivery dates on one order is the correct model for staggered fulfilment — not separate orders per timeline (which fragments the customer's one purchase), not remarks (which no report reads), not holding the whole order hostage to its slowest line.

The order also fixes the commercial terms for the rest of the cycle: rates, taxes, payment terms — which the Maintain-Same-Rate setting then defends downstream.

lessons.title: What submission does
lessons.html:
Submitting a Sales Order is not filing paperwork — it changes system state in two ways every seller must understand:

1. Stock intent is committed. The ordered quantities appear as reserved against the warehouse. Reserved stock is not deducted (deduction is the Delivery Note's job, next module), and nothing transfers to the customer yet — but everyone SEES the promise: another salesperson checking availability sees actual-minus-reserved; the planner sees demand; procurement sees what must be bought. Reservation is the mechanism that stops two reps selling the same last 50 cartons.

2. The fulfilment ledger opens. The order now tracks, per row: quantity ordered, delivered so far, billed so far. Every Delivery Note and Sales Invoice made FROM the order counts these down automatically. That's why creating downstream documents from the order matters mechanically, not just for convenience: a delivery note typed from scratch doesn't count against anything, and the order will insist those goods are still owed. The remaining quantities count down as Delivery Notes are made from the order — not as payments arrive, not as time passes, not as stock is purchased.

lessons.title: Status language & control
lessons.html:
Order status is a compact sentence about what remains owed. The vocabulary:

  • To Deliver and Bill — freshly submitted; both obligations outstanding. Every order starts here.
  • To Bill — delivered in full, not yet invoiced. Goods gone; money not asked for.
  • To Deliver — invoiced first (advance-billing deals), goods still owed.
  • Completed — both done.

Two manual controls change an order's course:

  • Hold — pauses the order. Credit trouble, stock uncertainty, customer says "wait": Hold keeps the commitment intact but stops fulfilment. Not cancellation, not closure — a pause.
  • Close — ends it early, deliberately. The classic case: customer took 80 of 100 and will take no more. Closing the order releases the reserved stock for the remaining 20 and removes the order from every pending-delivery list — the honest end. Cancelling would falsify history (the 80 DID happen); deleting rows mutilates a submitted document; delivering 20 to scrap is absurd. Close is the answer — know this cold.

Amending: submitted documents don't get edited — they get cancelled and Amended, which creates the next revision (same number, -1 suffix) with the original preserved in history. Quantities changed, rows added: cancel → Amend → adjust → resubmit. Never a fresh order pretending the first didn't exist, and never database surgery.

lessons.title: Delivery tolerance
lessons.html:
Paper says 100; the pallet holds 102. Real warehouses overship slightly — bulk goods, pack rounding, good-faith extras — and the system must decide whether to allow it.

The Over Delivery/Receipt Allowance % answers it: set on the item (per-product tolerance) or globally in settings (the fallback), it defines how much a delivery may exceed the ordered quantity before ZhiftERP blocks the delivery note. Allowance 5% on an order of 100 → deliveries up to 105 pass; 106 is refused. Shipping 102 against 100 is permitted when the allowance covers the 2% — not never, not because the driver insists, and the invoice has nothing to do with it.

Choosing the number is a policy decision, per item class: zero tolerance is right for serialized electronics — every unit has an identity, 100 means exactly 100 serials; slack there is how phones vanish. Bulk cement, produce, consumables earn a few percent, because blocking a 101st bag helps nobody. "Zero for everything" strangles the warehouse; "slack for everything" leaks serialized stock. Match tolerance to the nature of the goods.

delivery.title: Selling 5 — Delivery Notes & Returns
delivery.desc: Where stock actually moves: delivery notes from orders, partial shipments, statuses, sales returns, packing slips, and serial/batch discipline.

lessons.title: The document that moves stock
lessons.html:
Everything before this module was promise; the Delivery Note is physics. Submitting a Delivery Note deducts stock from the warehouse. Fix the timeline in your head permanently: quotation moves nothing, Sales Order reserves, Delivery Note deducts, invoice moves money, payment settles it. When a client asks "why does my stock report still show those goods?", the first question is "has the delivery note been submitted?"

Creation discipline: from the Sales Order — Create > Delivery Note — never from scratch, never by copying an old DN. Three reasons: quantities, rates and taxes flow correctly; the order's fulfilment ledger counts down (a from-scratch DN counts against nothing, and the order will insist the goods are still owed); and the document chain stays auditable — this DN fulfils that order fulfils that quotation.

The DN records the warehouse each row ships from, the shipping address chosen from the customer's addresses, and the transporter details when you need them on the waybill. Its print format IS the delivery document your driver carries and the customer's gate signs.

lessons.title: Partial delivery & status
lessons.html:
Orders rarely ship whole. The mechanics of shipping 60 of 100 today:

Create the DN from the order and edit the quantity down to 60 on the row. Submit. The order's ledger now shows 60 delivered, 40 remaining — and here is the part that makes the system trustworthy: the next DN created from that order offers exactly the 40 remaining. Not 100 again (no double-shipping), not whatever someone types from memory. The order arithmetic is authoritative.

Where to see undelivered backlog: remaining-to-deliver is order-side data — read it on the Sales Order itself or across all orders in the order-analysis reports (Selling 6 names them). The DN list can't tell you what HASN'T shipped; only orders know what they're still owed.

DN status: a submitted DN reads To Bill until a Sales Invoice covers it, then Completed. "To Bill" on a DN is a small alarm: goods have left the building and nobody has asked for money yet — a list of To-Bill DNs older than a few days is revenue leaking.

Direction of creation can also reverse: in advance-billing flows where the Sales Invoice came first, the DN is created against the invoice — same chain, opposite order. A DN is never made against a quotation, a lead, or a price list.

lessons.title: Sales returns
lessons.html:
Goods come back — wrong spec, damaged in transit, customer over-ordered. The clean reversal has two halves, and this module owns the stock half.

The Sales Return is a Delivery Note with Is Return ticked, created against the original DN, carrying negative quantities. Submitting it moves stock back INTO the warehouse — the exact mirror of the outbound. Three properties make this the only correct method:

  • Traceability — the return references the precise original shipment: which DN, which batch, which serials came back. An unlinked "stock adjustment" restores quantity but destroys the story; deleting the original DN falsifies history; a purchase receipt is a different doctype for a different trading partner entirely.
  • Valuation — the return re-enters stock at the correct value, because it knows what left.
  • Partiality — return 5 of the 60 shipped; the negative rows say exactly which 5.

The money half is a separate document: the customer's refund or credit is the credit note — a return Sales Invoice — covered in Selling 7. Stock reverses on the return DN; money reverses on the credit note; the two link to their respective originals. One event, two ledgers, two documents. The return DN itself does not touch the customer's balance, and cash from the driver is not an accounting system.

lessons.title: Packing slips, serials & batches
lessons.html:
Three companions to the DN that turn "we shipped it" into an operation:

Packing Slip — created against the DN, it lists cartons and their contents: case 1 of 3 holds these items, case 2 holds those. Its audience is the driver and the receiving gate — the people who count boxes, not lines. It does not replace the DN (no stock effect), charges nothing, and reserves nothing; it is the physical-handling companion. Multi-carton B2B shipments without packing slips produce gate disputes; with them, the gate ticks cartons and signs.

Serial numbers — an item flagged serialized requires the exact serial numbers being shipped entered on the DN row. Not "any 10 units": THESE ten, by identity. That per-unit identity is what powers warranty claims ("was this unit ours, and when did it ship?") and theft control. It requires no manager approval and no batch number — it requires the serials.

Batches — batch-tracked items (pharma, food) record which batch each DN row shipped. The payoff is the recall question: "which customers received batch B-204?" — answerable in seconds by searching DNs for the batch, because batch numbers are recorded on each Delivery Note. Not because drivers keep notebooks, and not from invoices (money documents, not movement documents). For your pharmacy clients this is regulatory survival: NAFDAC recall queries are DN queries.
