taxes_invoicing.title: Selling 6 — Taxes, Pricing Rules & Invoicing
taxes_invoicing.desc: VAT done right, inclusive vs exclusive, item tax overrides, pricing rules and discounts, the Sales Invoice, payments, credit notes — and the reports that watch it all.

lessons.title: Sales taxes & VAT
lessons.html:
Tax setup is write-once, apply-everywhere. The Sales Taxes and Charges Template defines the tax rows a selling document carries — for Nigerian trade, a template with one row: VAT, 7.5%, On Net Total, posting to your VAT output liability account. Selecting that template on any quotation, order, or invoice applies VAT uniformly — never typed per row, never inferred from the customer master, never a pricing rule's job. Build once; select everywhere; when FIRS changes the rate, change one template.

Item-level overrides: not everything is standard-rated. A zero-rated or exempt item sitting on an otherwise VAT-able invoice is handled by an Item Tax Template attached to that item, overriding the document rate for that row only — 7.5% on the taxable rows, 0% on the exempt one, one invoice, correct return. You do not delete the document's tax row (breaking the other rows), split invoices, or fake it with a discount.

Inclusive vs exclusive — get the arithmetic reflexive: exclusive (the default) adds tax on top: rate ₦1,000 → total ₦1,075. Inclusive (a checkbox on the tax row) means the entered rate already CONTAINS the tax: ₦1,075 inclusive at 7.5% = ₦1,000 net + ₦75 VAT (divide by 1.075). Retail prices are typically quoted inclusive; B2B exclusive. Mixing them up misstates either your price (charging tax on tax) or your VAT return (remitting less than collected) — both expensive.

lessons.title: Pricing rules & discounts
lessons.html:
Two instruments cut prices; a professional keeps them in the right hands.

Pricing Rules — policy, automated. A Pricing Rule applies a discount (percentage or amount) or a special rate automatically when its conditions match. Conditions span: what (item, item group, brand), who (customer, customer group, territory), how much (quantity brackets — 50+ cartons), and when (valid from/to). So "10% off cartons of 50+ for Distributors in Q4" is built ONCE as a rule and fires itself on every qualifying order — not circulated as a memo (memos get forgotten and misapplied), not manually edited per order (inconsistent, invisible), not a per-quarter clone of the price list. Rules can stack with priorities when several match; keep rules few and legible.

Manual discounts — exceptions, visible. Per document there is an Additional Discount (on the grand or net total) and per-row rate cuts. These exist for the genuinely exceptional negotiation. The discipline: policy lives in price lists and pricing rules; manual discounts stay rare and visible — reportable exceptions, not the everyday pricing method, not hidden inside doctored rates, and not banned outright (real negotiations exist). When "exceptional" discounts appear on every order, pricing has left the system and moved into WhatsApp — the moment to rebuild the rules.

lessons.title: The Sales Invoice & getting paid
lessons.html:
The Sales Invoice is the accounting event of the cycle: submitting it books revenue and the customer's receivable into the ledgers. Not the order (a promise), not the DN (goods movement), not the payment (settlement of what the invoice created) — the INVOICE is where money becomes real on the books. Selling 7 dedicates a full module to its depths; here is the working core.

Creation: from the Sales Order (billing ahead of or with delivery) or from the Delivery Note (billing exactly what shipped) — the same no-retyping spine. Quantities, rates, taxes flow; the order's billed-quantity ledger counts down.

Getting paid: money arrives as a Payment Entry — full payment closes the invoice; a partial leaves it Partly Paid with the outstanding visible; and one customer payment covering several invoices is ONE Payment Entry allocated across all of them — not three separate entries, not a bare journal, and certainly not a credit note (that reverses revenue, the opposite of receiving it!).

Status = the collections story: Unpaid → Partly Paid → Paid; and the moment the due date passes unpaid, Overdue. The invoice list filtered to Overdue is your collections worklist. Not "Late", not "Blocked" — Overdue.

lessons.title: Credit notes & the watching reports
lessons.html:
The credit note: when goods return or an invoice must be corrected, revenue reverses via a Sales Invoice with Is Return ticked, made against the original invoice — negative amounts pulling revenue and receivable back, linked to what they reverse. Not a special letter, not cancelling the invoice (history falsified), not a "negative payment". It mirrors the return DN: stock reverses on the return Delivery Note; money reverses on the credit note — one physical event, two ledgers, two linked documents. This pairing is what auditors — and FIRS — expect to find.

The three watching reports — read them weekly, not at quarter-end panic:

  • Sales Analytics — revenue sliced by customer, item, item group, territory over time. Growth, mix, and the customer quietly shrinking.
  • Sales Order Analysis — ordered vs delivered vs billed across all open orders: the delivery backlog in one screen. This, not the DN list, answers "what have we promised and not shipped?"
  • Accounts Receivable — who owes what, aged into buckets (0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days). The ageing is the point: ₦5m owed 15 days is business; ₦5m owed 95 days is a problem with a name. This is the receivables instrument — not Sales Analytics, not the stock ledger.

A sales professional who reads these three weekly manages a book; one who doesn't, gets managed by it.

sales_invoice.title: Selling 7 — The Sales Invoice, Payments & Collections
sales_invoice.desc: The accounting event in full: creating invoices from orders and delivery notes, what submission books, due dates and payment terms, Payment Entry mechanics including advances and allocation, credit notes, and the receivables discipline that turns sales into cash.

lessons.title: The invoice as the accounting event
lessons.html:
Everything before it was commitment and movement; the Sales Invoice is where money becomes real on the books. Submitting it books revenue and the customer's receivable in the general ledger, dated by the invoice's posting date. Nothing else in the cycle does this: the order promises, the DN moves goods, the payment (later) settles what the invoice created. If the question is "when do the books recognise this sale?", the answer is always: at invoice submission.

Creation paths, chosen by flow:

  • From the Sales Order — billing ahead of or alongside delivery (advance-billing deals, services).
  • From the Delivery Note — billing exactly what shipped: quantities on the invoice are the quantities that actually left. For partial-delivery trade this is the honest path — you invoice the 60 that went, not the 100 ordered.
  • Standalone — for genuinely document-less sales; rare in disciplined B2B.

Two dates, two meanings — never conflate them: the posting date is when the books record the sale; the due date is when the customer must pay. The due date is not "posting + 30 always" and not the delivery date: it is computed from the Payment Terms — Net 30, 50% advance / balance on delivery, end-of-following-month — which the invoice inherits from the customer or the order. Terms belong on the master or the order precisely so nobody improvises them at billing time; the seller's job is to make sure they're set BEFORE the first invoice, not negotiated after it.

lessons.title: Statuses & the collections story
lessons.html:
An invoice's status is the collections narrative in one word:

  • Unpaid — submitted, no money yet.
  • Partly Paid — some money allocated, outstanding remains. A ₦2m receipt against a ₦5m invoice leaves it here — visibly ₦3m short, not "Paid", not still "Unpaid".
  • Paid — outstanding cleared.
  • Overdue — the due date passed while unpaid (or partly paid). Automatic, merciless, useful.
  • Credit Note Issued — a return invoice has been raised against it (lesson 4).

The worklist habit: the invoice list filtered to Overdue, sorted oldest-first, IS collections. Open it weekly. Every entry gets an action — a call, a statement, a dated next step on the Duty Board pipeline — because an overdue invoice nobody is chasing is a donation.

The Update Stock special case — know it to avoid double-movement: an invoice with Update Stock ticked moves inventory itself — it plays both money document and delivery note. Its legitimate home is flows that skip the DN: counter sales, service jobs with materials. The trap: tick Update Stock on an invoice made FROM a Delivery Note and stock moves twice — once at the DN, once at the invoice — and your stock report is now lying. Standard flow: DN moves stock, invoice moves money, Update Stock stays off.

lessons.title: Payment Entry mechanics
lessons.html:
Money arrives in every shape; the Payment Entry records them all. Make it FROM the invoice (Create > Payment) so the reference and amounts pre-fill. The shapes:

  • Full payment — allocates the whole outstanding; invoice → Paid.
  • Partial payment — allocate what came; invoice → Partly Paid, outstanding visible. Repeat until cleared.
  • One payment, many invoices — a customer's single ₦12m transfer settling four invoices is ONE Payment Entry with four allocation rows, splitting the amount across the references. Never four fabricated entries for one bank line — reconciliation must match the bank statement line-for-line.
  • Advance payment — money BEFORE any invoice exists (your enterprise 50%-upfront deals): a Payment Entry taken against the customer, sitting as an advance on their account; when the invoice is later raised, the advance is allocated to it. Not "wait for the invoice to bank the cheque", not a negative invoice, not a discount.
  • Write-off — the customer pays ₦1,999,820 against ₦2m. Chasing ₦180 forever costs more than ₦180: within your configured write-off limit, the Payment Entry writes off the difference and closes the invoice honestly. Never edit the invoice total to match the shortfall.

On every entry: Mode of Payment (transfer, POS, cash, cheque) and the receiving bank account — filled correctly at entry, these make month-end bank reconciliation a matching exercise instead of archaeology.

lessons.title: Credit notes & receivables discipline
lessons.html:
Correcting a submitted invoice: a submitted invoice with a wrong rate is never edited and never deleted — the audit trail is the point of submission. The correct fix is a credit note against it, then re-invoice correctly: the credit note is a Sales Invoice with Is Return ticked, made against the original, reversing revenue and receivable with negative amounts; the original's status flips to Credit Note Issued — permanently tying reversal to reversed. Then a fresh, correct invoice goes out. Auditors and FIRS expect exactly this pattern: every figure that ever hit the ledger, plus the visible document that unwound it. "Journal patches" to fix invoice errors are how audits go from routine to forensic.

For returned goods the credit note is the money half of the pair from Selling 5: stock came back on the return DN; the customer's balance comes back on the credit note.

Receivables discipline — the weekly trinity:

  • Accounts Receivable report — who owes what, aged into buckets (0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+). Age is risk: read the right-hand columns first.
  • Statement of Account — sent to each credit customer monthly. Customers dispute what they see once a quarter; they pay what they see every month.
  • A dated next step for every overdue invoice — in this house that means the Duty Board pipeline's next-step discipline, applied to collections: no overdue invoice without a named person and a date on its follow-up. Hope is not a collections strategy.

Selling ends when the money is in the bank. This module is the difference between revenue and cash.

advanced.title: Selling 8 — Advanced Selling: Settings, Bundles, Blanket Orders & Sales Teams
advanced.desc: The advanced layer: Selling Settings in depth, Product Bundles, Blanket Orders for long-term rate agreements, and the two sales-team structures — Sales Person (internal, contribution and targets) and Sales Partner (external channel and commission).

lessons.title: Selling Settings — the full tour
lessons.html:
Selling Settings is where selling policy becomes system behaviour. A consultant should be able to defend every switch on this screen to a client's managing director. The tour:

Naming: Customer Naming By — Customer Name makes the record's ID the name itself ("Alpha Pharmacy"); Naming Series issues CUST-00042 style IDs. The decision rule: chains and portfolios with duplicate or near-duplicate names need the series — a retailer with "Adepoju Stores" in three cities cannot key records by name without collisions. Series naming keeps identity unambiguous forever; the display name remains human.

Defaults: Default Customer Group, Territory, and Selling Price List pre-fill new records and documents. Set them to your commonest case so hurried data entry lands correctly instead of blank.

The discipline switches — each answers a client policy question:

  • "Can we stop staff typing special prices?" → untick Allow User to Edit Price List Rate. Rates then come ONLY from Item Price records; the rate field is read-only on documents. The single strongest anti-discount control that exists — stronger than memos, smaller price lists, or threats.
  • "Can we prevent selling below cost?" → Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate: blocks a selling rate below the item's purchase cost at the point of entry. Margin protection built into the keyboard, not discovered in a month-end report.
  • "Can the agreed rate change between order and invoice?" → Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle, whose companion action setting chooses the response to a drift: Stop (hard block) or Warning (allow but flag). Strict shops choose Stop; shops with legitimate mid-cycle repricing choose Warning. Not silence, not auto-correction, not an email.
  • Allow Item to be Added Multiple Times — same item on two rows (standard + promo rate), from Selling 1.
  • The global over-delivery allowance — the fallback that Selling 4's per-item tolerance overrides.

When a policy question arrives, check this screen before writing a customisation — nine times in ten, the switch already exists.

lessons.title: Product Bundles
lessons.html:
You price as ONE thing but pick as MANY things: a "Pharmacy Starter Pack" at ₦450,000 that is really shelving units + a barcode scanner + a receipt printer. The Product Bundle is the correct model — never a workaround stock item whose contents live in someone's head and whose warehouse quantity nobody can honestly count.

The construction:

  • The parent item — created as a normal item BUT non-stock: Maintain Stock UNTICKED. The parent never has warehouse quantity; it is a commercial identity, not a physical one. (Not "a stock item with quantity", not necessarily serialized, not a service.)
  • The bundle definition — the Product Bundle record lists the parent and its child items with quantities: 4 × shelf unit, 1 × scanner, 1 × printer.
  • Pricing — an Item Price for the PARENT on your selling list: ₦450,000. Children need no selling price for the bundle to work.

The mechanics at each document: on the quotation and the invoice, the customer sees ONE line at the parent's price — clean commercial presentation, no per-child price exposure. On the Delivery Note, the bundle EXPLODES into its packed items — the children appear as the packed-items list, and it is the CHILDREN that move stock from the warehouse: 4 shelves, 1 scanner, 1 printer deducted; the parent deducts nothing (it has nothing to deduct). Price lives on the parent; picking lives on the children. Hampers, promo packs, starter kits, installation kits — the pattern is everywhere in Nigerian retail; model it once, correctly.

lessons.title: Blanket Orders
lessons.html:
A customer says: "we'll take 10,000 cartons over the next six months — what's your best rate?" You agree ₦820. This is more than a quotation (they've committed, not enquired) and less than a Sales Order (they don't want 10,000 cartons delivered Tuesday). It is a Blanket Order: a long-term rate-and-quantity agreement consumed over time.

Creating it: the Blanket Order carries the customer, the items with agreed quantities and agreed rates, and the from/to dates of the agreement. Submitting it creates no reservation and moves no stock — it establishes the commercial frame.

Drawing against it: each real purchase becomes an ordinary Sales Order referencing the blanket order — and two things happen automatically: the order row inherits the agreed ₦820 rate (nobody negotiates twice, nobody "forgets" the deal rate), and the blanket order records the drawdown — ordered-so-far against committed. Not just the quantity copies, and the delivery date is per-order business, not the blanket's.

Reading the commitment: "how much of the 10,000 remains?" is read from the blanket order itself — its ordered-vs-committed quantities — not from the customer's memory, the last invoice, or stock levels. Both sides see the same consumption truth, which is precisely what makes volume agreements governable.

Blanket vs the alternatives: one giant 10,000-carton Sales Order reserves half a warehouse for months and lies about delivery intent. A quotation stretched to six-month validity is an offer awaiting an answer pretending to be an agreement being consumed — wrong document, wrong semantics. A pricing rule gives the rate but tracks no commitment. The blanket order is the instrument built for exactly this shape of deal — your Montaigne-class volume agreements belong here.

lessons.title: Sales Person — the internal team
lessons.html:
Sales Person models YOUR OWN sales force — and models it as a tree, not a flat list: Sales Director → Regional Managers → Field Reps. The tree is the point: results roll up the hierarchy, so the Lagos region's number is the sum of its reps' numbers and the director's number is the company, without anyone building spreadsheets.

Assignment on transactions: selling documents carry a Sales Team section where one or MORE sales persons are attached, each with a contribution % — and the percentages sum to 100. A deal worked by two reps splits 60/40: reports then credit each with their contributed share of the revenue, never double-counting the deal. Not two invoices for one sale, not a note in remarks, not two "sales partners" (wrong concept entirely — next lesson).

Targets: each sales person can carry targets by item group and period (monthly, quarterly). Actuals accrue from their assigned transactions.

The report: Sales Person-wise Transaction Summary — each person's transactions, contributed amounts, and performance against target. League tables, commission calculations, and performance conversations all read from here.

The consultant's honest answer — when a client asks "can we see sales by rep?": only if sales persons are assigned on the transactions. The report is arithmetic over assignments; installing it changes nothing, targets alone measure nothing, partners are a different object. The discipline of assignment precedes the report — configure the tree, make the Sales Team section mandatory in the client's process, and THEN the question answers itself weekly.

lessons.title: Sales Partner — the external channel
lessons.html:
A Sales Partner is a business OUTSIDE your company that brings you deals — a reseller, a referral agent, a channel distributor, an implementation partner who sources clients. The record carries the partner's identity, type, and — the operative field — a commission rate.

On transactions: select the Sales Partner on a Sales Order or Sales Invoice and two things happen: the deal is stamped as that channel's business (channel revenue becomes reportable), and the document computes the total commission at the partner's rate — the liability you owe them for the introduction, calculated per deal, automatically.

The distinction to keep razor-sharp — Person vs Partner:

  • Sales Person = internal staff: a tree, contribution percentages summing to 100, targets, performance management.
  • Sales Partner = an external business: a flat entity, a commission %, a payable relationship.

They are not the same thing with different names, commission is not what separates them (both can drive earnings), and a partner is not a customer. And a single transaction can legitimately carry BOTH: your rep (Sales Person, 100% contribution) worked a deal that a referral firm (Sales Partner, 5% commission) introduced.

Paying partners: commissions are settled from the Sales Partner-wise Transaction Summary — the system's own totals of each channel's business and accrued commission. Pay partners from the report, not from their claims: when the partner's invoice says ₦2.4m and your summary says ₦2.1m, the summary — built from the actual stamped transactions — is the negotiating position. Channel programs die of over-payment and under-tracking; this report prevents both.
